newsitem.title: GERMANY: Electronic rival nears for German trading floor.
newsitem.headline: Electronic rival nears for German trading floor.

text.p: The death-knell sounded for traditional floor trading in Germany on Thursday as the stock exchange said it would launch the first stage of a fully electronic dealing system at the end of 1997.

The 150 million mark ($89 million) Xetra system will supplant Germany's IBIS screen-based trading system this year. It will deal at first only with wholesale orders, but expand by the end of 1998 to become a full competitor to traditional floor trading.

"The countdown is on. With the introduction of the Xetra trading system at the end of the year, Deutsche Boerse (German stock exchange) will introduce a new era for German securities trading," bourse chairman Werner Seifert told reporters.
"We are fully within the timetable and fully on our budget target," he added.

Fully electronic trade is seen in Germany as a major step toward a more efficient, and -- crucially -- a more internationally competitive environment for securities and as a means of boosting liquidity in smaller shares.
"The electronics will make it easier for new participants to enter the market. More participants, however simplistic it sounds, mean more liquidity," Seifert said.

The implications for brokers on the trading floor are less rosy. Xetra, an order-driven system offering automatic price matches, is designed to create a level playing field by eliminating the need for intermediaries.
Seifert declined to predict how long traditional floor trading could survive such competition.
"It's not worthwhile to speculate," he said. "Nobody wants to take legal means to abolish the trading floor ... it will remain as long as there are two people who want to come there and trade."

But Seifert said he could well imagine that Germany would follow London's lead, where the introduction of electronic trading after the 1986 Big Bang market reforms gradually caused floor trade to die out.
But he added that floor trade was a useful back-up if technical problems -- which have been relatively common on the German bourse lately -- disrupted Xetra.

The new system will be introduced in stages, gradually broadening to cover the bulk of Germany's smaller listed securities by the end of 1998. This will make it a full competitor for the three-hour bourse trading session.

The bourse says Xetra will be cheaper, faster and more transparent than either IBIS or floor trade, with a data feed giving market participants detailed displays on current prices and the background to them.

The move to fully electronic trade is the latest in a series of stock market reforms as Frankfurt pushes to develop its status as a significant international financial centre, particularly as the European single currency looms.

The DTB futures and options exchange set up in 1990, causing a minor revolution in a country where derivatives trade had formerly been outlawed as gambling, followed soon after the limited IBIS electronic trade.
Legislation passed in mid-1994 tightened requirements on publishing market-moving corporate news and criminalised insider trading for the first time.

The fact that the Xetra system's full launch was timed to match the planned introduction of the euro in January 1999 was pure coincidence, Seifert said, but he added: "I think that's a positive thing."

Seifert conceded the new electronic system in itself had limited power to change the German share market significantly, which is still regarded as acutely underdeveloped compared with the British or U.S. markets.

"The system cannot at one fell swoop solve problems that have their root in totally different reasons, such as an inadequate share culture, a lack of market sophistication. That would be too much to expect," he said.
